lead: At one fixed frequency, every sinusoid in a circuit has the same ω. Only its peak and its phase change from point to point. A phasor stores those two numbers as one complex number: a vector frozen at t = 0. Adding two sinusoids then becomes adding two vectors. This turns differential equations into algebra with j. Phasors are used in AC circuit analysis, power calculations, transformers, machines and three-phase systems. The price is that the method works only in the sinusoidal steady state, at one frequency at a time.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for peak, ω and phase, and Unit 1 for the R, L, C voltage-current relations.

blocks.text: Euler's relation is the bridge. It says e<sup>jθ</sup> = cos θ + j sin θ, with j² = −1. A cosine wave is v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> cos(ωt + φ). Write it as Re{V<sub>m</sub> e<sup>jφ</sup> e<sup>jωt</sup>}. The factor e<sup>jωt</sup> spins at the supply frequency ω and is the same for every sinusoid in the circuit. Drop it. What remains is the phasor V = V<sub>m</sub>∠φ. Here V<sub>m</sub> is the peak voltage in volts, φ is the phase angle in degrees or radians, ω is the angular frequency in rad/s, and t is time in seconds. The phasor is not the waveform. It is the waveform frozen at t = 0, with only magnitude and phase kept. To return, multiply by e<sup>jωt</sup> and take the real part for cosine reference, or the imaginary part for sine reference.

Sine reference: v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ), so the phasor is V<sub>m</sub>∠φ on sine reference. Cosine reference: v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> cos(ωt + φ), so the phasor is V<sub>m</sub>∠φ on cosine reference. The two conventions differ by 90°. Since sin θ = cos(θ − 90°), a sine-reference phasor of 20∠0° is 20∠−90° on cosine reference. Pick the convention your textbook uses and state it. Some Indian syllabi use sine; many use cosine. Never switch midway.
RMS phasor: magnitude = Vm/√2. Use RMS magnitudes when the answer feeds a power calculation (see 3.5). Peak and RMS values cannot be added in one sum. Below, magnitudes are peak unless marked RMS.
v(t) = Re{V<sub>m</sub> e<sup>jφ</sup> e<sup>jωt</sup>} → V = V<sub>m</sub>∠φ
blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is peak volts; φ is phase in degrees or radians; ω is rad/s; t is seconds; V is the phasor.

blocks.text: j is the imaginary unit, j = √−1. On the complex plane, multiplying any phasor by j rotates it counterclockwise by 90°. Check: 1 × j = j, and j × j = −1, which is 1 rotated by 180°. So jV has the same magnitude as V and angle φ + 90°.

Differentiation becomes multiplication by jω. Start with Vm ej(ωt+φ). Its time derivative is jω times the same expression. The common ejωt cancels, so d/dt → jω on phasors. Integration → 1/(jω) = −j/ω. This is why the inductor relation v = L di/dt becomes V = jωL I, and the capacitor relation i = C dv/dt becomes I = jωC V. Those element relations become impedances in 3.3.
V = a + jb = r∠θ; r = √(a² + b²); θ = tan<sup>−1</sup>(b/a)
blocks.where: a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, r is the magnitude, θ is the angle; choose the quadrant from the signs of a and b.

blocks.text: Complex algebra refresher. Add or subtract by real parts and imaginary parts separately. Multiply by multiplying magnitudes and adding angles. Divide by dividing magnitudes and subtracting angles. Some syllabi call all this the j-notation or complex representation.
A phasor diagram draws each phasor as an arrow from the origin. Arrow length is magnitude; arrow angle is phase. The diagram is a snapshot at t = 0, not a picture of the wires.

Choose the common quantity as reference. In a series circuit the current is the same through every element, so draw I at 0°. Then place each element voltage at its angle: V<sub>R</sub> in phase with I, V<sub>L</sub> leading I by 90°, V<sub>C</sub> lagging I by 90°. In a parallel circuit the voltage is common, so draw V at 0° and place the branch currents by their element relations. For a capacitor, I leads V by 90°, so the current arrow is at +90° when V is at 0°. For an inductor, I lags V by 90°.

Lead and lag come from the sign of φ<sub>v</sub> − φ<sub>i</sub>. If φ<sub>v</sub> − φ<sub>i</sub> > 0, voltage leads current. If φ<sub>v</sub> − φ<sub>i</sub> < 0, voltage lags current. The words alone confuse; the sign does not. For a pure inductor, φ<sub>v</sub> − φ<sub>i</sub> = +90°. For a pure capacitor, φ<sub>v</sub> − φ<sub>i</sub> = −90°. For a resistor, it is 0°.

Add phasors tip to tail. Put the tail of the second at the head of the first. The resultant runs from the origin to the final head. Subtraction adds the negative phasor. The figure draws the worked example: 20 V at 0° plus 15 V at 60° gives a dashed resultant of 30.4 V at 25.3°. The resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two phasors.

figure.caption: Tip-to-tail addition of the two series voltages: 20 V at 0° plus 15 V at 60° gives the dashed resultant 30.4 V at 25.3°. The dashed arrow is the diagonal of the parallelogram.

spec.aria: Two phasors drawn tip to tail, 20 V at 0 degrees and then 15 V at 60 degrees, with the dashed resultant from the origin at 30.4 V and 25.3 degrees.

examples.question: Two series-connected AC sources apply v1 = 20 sin(314t) V and v2 = 15 sin(314t + 60°) V. Find the total voltage v = v1 + v2 as a single sinusoid. Use the sine reference.
steps: At ω = 314 rad/s both waves have the same frequency. Write phasors on sine reference: V1 = 20∠0° V peak; V2 = 15∠60° V peak.
Convert V2 to rectangular: V2 = 15 cos 60° + j15 sin 60° = 7.5 + j12.99 V.
Add real and imaginary parts: V = V1 + V2 = (20 + 7.5) + j12.99 = 27.5 + j12.99 V.
Angle: φ = tan⁻¹(12.99/27.5) = 25.3°. Both parts are positive, so the angle is in the first quadrant.
Return to time domain: v(t) = 30.4 sin(314t + 25.3°) V.
examples.answer: The total voltage is 30.4 V peak with phase 25.3°, so v(t) = 30.4 sin(314t + 25.3°) V.
examples.check:
import math
V1 = 20.0
V2 = 15.0
phi2 = math.radians(60.0)
x = V1 + V2 * math.cos(phi2)
y = V2 * math.sin(phi2)
mag = math.hypot(x, y)
ang = math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x))
print(round(mag, 1))
print(round(ang, 1))

traps: Switching from sine to cosine reference in the middle of a solution and forgetting the 90° shift. A waveform that is 10∠30° on sine reference is 10∠−60° on cosine reference.
Adding a peak phasor to an RMS phasor, or adding magnitudes 20 and 15 to get 35. Phasors add as vectors; 20∠0° + 15∠60° is 30.4∠25.3°, not 35∠60°.
Using tan⁻¹(b/a) without the quadrant. If a is negative, the angle is in the second or third quadrant, so add or subtract 180° as needed.
Mixing up lead and lag. Use the sign of φ_v − φ_i: positive means voltage leads current; negative means voltage lags current. A capacitor has φ_v − φ_i = −90°, so its current leads its voltage.

quiz.q: What two quantities does a phasor keep from a sinusoid at a fixed frequency?
quiz.a: Magnitude (peak or RMS) and phase angle. It drops the common e^(jωt) rotation.

quiz.q: Why does multiplying a phasor by j rotate it by 90°?
quiz.a: j = 1∠90°. Multiplying magnitudes and adding angles gives r∠θ × 1∠90° = r∠(θ + 90°).

quiz.q: Add v1 = 8 sin(ωt) V and v2 = 6 sin(ωt + 90°) V on sine reference.
Two phasors both have magnitude 5, at 0° and 120°. Can their sum have magnitude 10? Explain with the tip-to-tail picture.
quiz.a: No. 5∠0° + 5∠120° = 5 + (−2.5 + j4.33) = 2.5 + j4.33 = 5∠60°. The triangle is equilateral; the resultant has magnitude 5, not 10. Magnitudes add to 10 only when the phasors are in phase.

quiz.q: A textbook uses cosine reference. A voltage is 10 sin(ωt + 30°) V. Write its phasor.
quiz.a: sin θ = cos(θ − 90°), so the angle is 30° − 90° = −60°. Phasor = 10∠−60° V peak.

quiz.q: In a series RL circuit the current is the reference phasor. What is the sign of φ_v − φ_i for the inductor voltage, and does that voltage lead or lag the current?
quiz.a: For an inductor, voltage leads current by 90°, so φ_v − φ_i = +90°. The inductor voltage leads the current.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power systems, synchrophasors from phasor measurement units compare voltage angles across the grid at GPS time stamps, so operators can see stress before a blackout. In drives and control, the complex frequency response V(jω)/I(jω) is evaluated from the phasor circuit to design compensators. In signal processing, the same idea becomes the discrete Fourier transform bin at one frequency. Search next: phasor measurement unit, synchrophasor, complex frequency response, j-notation.
